props.title: Andrei Rublev

sections.content: Andrei Rublev (1966) stands as Tarkovsky's monumental exploration of art, faith, and medieval Russia. Shot in stark black-and-white (except for its stunning color epilogue), this 3-hour epic follows the legendary 15th-century icon painter through a series of episodes that test his artistic and spiritual convictions. Like Tarkovsky's later Stalker (1979) and The Mirror (1975), the film eschews traditional narrative for a series of poetic, dreamlike sequences. The famous bell-casting finale, where a young bell-maker claims divine knowledge to create a massive church bell, serves as perhaps cinema's greatest metaphor for artistic creation under pressure.

sections.content: Tarkovsky's approach to historical cinema radically differs from conventional biopics. While films like Amadeus (1984) or The Agony and the Ecstasy (1965) dramatize artists' lives through traditional character arcs, Andrei Rublev presents history as a series of spiritual and philosophical challenges. The film's violence - including the brutal Tatar raids and pagan rituals - serves not as spectacle but as tests of faith. This approach influenced later meditative historical films like The Mission (1986) and Days of Heaven (1978). SUBHEAD: Visual Poetry and Religious Cinema

The film's visual language revolutionized religious cinema. Unlike the literal approach of The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965) or King of Kings (1961), Tarkovsky uses natural elements - rain, fire, snow, mud - as spiritual metaphors. This poetic style influenced directors like Terrence Malick, particularly in The Tree of Life (2011) and A Hidden Life (2019). The film's long takes and attention to texture created a template for contemplative cinema that echoes through works like Silent Light (2007) and Of Gods and Men (2010).
